The Internet of Things presents both a challenge and opportunity for identity management - a challenge because existing mechanisms for authentication & authorization must be extended and adapted for the particular constraints of devices (both legacy and new) and an opportunity because the devices that users more and more carry with them offer new abilities to enable a more seamless authentication experience for those users. Both of these aspects demand a consistent, cohesive and interoperable identity layer across IoT verticals, platforms, and protocols. Critically, we need an identity layer that acknowledges the full continuum of risk (and so appropriate security measures) that the IoT presents. Good security means knowing who entities (both device & user) are and what they should or should not be allowed to do. Good privacy requires that users will be able to control how their devices collect, store and share data. This talk will examine how existing & new tools (like OAuth, UMA, FIDO, and DLTs) may help meet these fundamental requirements for securing the IoT.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/identity-based-security-and-privacy-for-the-internet-of-things

While near-ultrasonic communications are gradually established as an alternative to Bluetooth and WiFi, the technology remains largely unregulated. This talk will go through the security challenges that the ecosystem faced from its inception, demonstrate its shortcomings and propose mitigations. The insights shared will inform potential adopters and those seeking to prevent security incidents.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn about near-ultrasonic communication technology and the surrounding ecosystem.
2: Explore security shortcomings, privacy issues and mitigations.
3: Discover past and future security incidents, coupled with relevant insights.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/the-good-the-bad-and-the-ugly-of-the-ultrasonic-communications-ecosystem

snippet.title: “No You May Not Have a Pony”—The Art of the Possible in Secure IAM Design
snippet.description:
Laura Hunter, Principal Program Manager, Microsoft
Heather Flanagan, Principal, Spherical Cow Consulting
Eve Maler, VP Innovation & Emerging Technology, ForgeRock
Sarah Squire, Senior Technical Architect, Ping Identity

In this interactive panel discussion, you’ll hear a diverse set of real-world perspectives on building security and standards into workable identity and access management solutions. The panel will share ways to have the right conversations with your customers and clients, to give you the best chance of creating design recommendations that actually work in the real world, not just in PowerPoint.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn how to disentangle executives’ IAM dreams from IT’s ability to execute.
2: Discuss “getting to yes” on users’ authentication and authorization experiences.
3: Get up to date on true best practices for identity standards and solutions.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/no-you-may-not-have-a-ponythe-art-of-the-possible-in-secure-iam-design

snippet.title: Turning Your Security Strategy Inside Out—Managing Insider Threat
snippet.description:
James Christiansen, VP, Global CISO, Teradata

We are accustomed to building security strategies that defined against external attackers. But you need to think differently when your attacker is inside the organization. Advanced attackers will masquerade as an insider, making it much more difficult to detect them. Hear the inside scoop from two top CISOs on how to use an insider threat model, as well as five steps to build a successful program.

Learning Objectives:
1: Understand the insider threat.
2: Learn how to create a threat risk model using kill chain analysis.
3: Develop an effective insider threat strategy.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18

snippet.title: Hacking Closed Networks
snippet.description:
Ira Winkler, President, Secure Mentem

When the USS John McCain collided with a freighter, there was speculation that the ship was hacked, but officials quickly stated it was impossible because the ship’s network was closed. That is not true. Stuxnet is one of many examples where attackers breached closed networks. This presentation will cover many ways closed networks can be compromised with examples, and how to prevent such attacks.Learning Objectives:1: Overcome the myth that closed networks can’t be hacked.2: Identify vulnerabilities allowing access to closed networks.3: Learn how to counter the vulnerabilities allowing compromise of closed networks.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/hacking-closed-networks

snippet.title: Cyberwar on a Shoestring: How Kim Jong Un Stole My Malware
snippet.description:
Kenneth Geers, Senior Research Scientist, Comodo Group

Global superpowers do not have a monopoly on cyber-warfare. Smaller nations and even nonstate actors may soon crash the party. This presentation will map a viable shortcut to the cyber-battlefield: reverse engineering advanced persistent threat (APT) digital weapons and replacing the payload with a custom Molotov cocktail. The strategic implications of this tactical chicanery are enormous.Learning Objectives:1: Explore a critical and often-overlooked aspect of cyber-warfare.2: Understand the ease with which re-weaponization of malware is possible.3: Learn how to prepare for this cutting-edge challenge.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/cyberwar-on-a-shoestring-how-kim-jong-un-stole-my-malware

snippet.title: Modern Exploitation: Owning All of the Things
snippet.description:
James Lyne, Head of R&D, SANS Institute

The difficulty level in exploiting vulnerabilities in modern applications and operating systems continues to increase. While the world of IoT allows many to relive the past, the current state of the Windows OS and applications such as IE, Edge and MS Office prove to be a challenge. This session will take an in-depth look at cutting-edge exploit techniques, as well as the state of modern mitigations.

Learning Objectives:
1: Gain a greater understanding of modern exploitation.
2: Learn to improve defenses by learning about the techniques used by attackers.
3: Understand the skill level required to identify and exploit bugs.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18/agenda/sessions/9243-modern-exploitation-owning-all-of-the-things

snippet.title: The Supply Chain Threat
snippet.description:
Richard George, Senior Advisor for Cyber Security, Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Lab

Over 41 years at NSA, Richard George saw a number of real-world supply chain attacks of various types. He will present some of these examples, then talk about the threat they presented and how the intentional weaknesses were inserted. He’ll also discuss the reaction when these attacks were brought to the attention of the companies and FBI, and what can be done to address this threat.

Learning Objectives:
1: Understand the significance and breadth of supply chain attacks.
2: Learn about mitigation methods to use today.
3: Learn from interesting stories of actual events.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18

snippet.description:
Cindy Compert, Cybersecurity Leader, US Public Sector Markets – CTO Data Privacy and Security, IBM Security

This session follows last year’s “Charting the Course to GDPR” five-phase implementation approach. This year’s menu will focus on sustainable practices gathered from working with clients and inside IBM. Topics include: GDPR myths and realities, program management, data mapping, classification and designing controls. As a bonus, Cindy Compert will share her favorite recipes. Bring your learning appetite!

Learning Objectives:
1: Understand the phases of a GDPR program and top readiness priorities.
2: Learn practical techniques for accelerating your GDPR program.
3: See working examples such as classification of personal data.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/get-cookin-with-gdprpractical-techniques-and-recipes-for-success

snippet.description:
Rick Howard, CSO, Palo Alto Networks
Richard Seiersen, SVP and Chief Information Security Officer, Lending Club

Network defenders have avoided quantitative risk assessments in the past because they are too hard: the math is complex and too many variables exist. What if we could use simple math tricks to reduce our uncertainty about ranges of possibilities and that would be enough to help us make risk decisions? Come find out how.

Learning Objectives:
1: Understand how to do high-precision risk assessments.
2: Understand simple math tricks for risk assessments.
3: Work through a real-world risk assessment.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18

snippet.description:
Cat Zakrzewski, Reporter, The Wall Street Journal
Bob Ackerman, Founder and Managing Director, AllegisCyber
David Brumley, CEO, ForAllSecure 
John N. Stewart, Senior Vice President, Chief Security and Trust Officer, Cisco

Cybersecurity attacks continue to morph and grow ever-more sophisticated and so, too, must the technology designed to shield organizations. Underneath the big picture are several technological pillars, both positive and negative. The panel will debate what these are, why they are significant and what threats they will be combating over the next three to five years.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn about new and improved cybersecurity technologies.
2: Learn about new and modified cybersecurity threats.
3: Learn about the pros and cons of AI and cybersecurity.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/over-the-horizon-cybersecurity-technologies-and-threats

snippet.description:

Jake Flomenberg, Partner, Accel  
Enrique Salem, Managing Director, Bain Capital Ventures
Ariel Tseitlin, Partner, Scale Venture Partners

VCs from Bain Capital Ventures, Scale Venture Partners and Accel, moderated by the WSJ’s Rob Sloan, unpack what’s top of mind for security investors and how they’re thinking about the market in the context of increased nation-state attacks and high-profile hacks like Equifax and the SEC, the shift in legal accountability of breaches, GDPR and the threat from initial coin offerings.

Learning Objectives:
1: Gain insight into how VCs are thinking about the security market and investments.
2: Learn how big hacks have altered the dynamic between boards and management teams.

snippet.title: Model-Driven Security: It’s Closer than You Think
snippet.description:
James Routh, CSO, Aetna

This session will explore five to seven different implementations of models (machine learning) that drive frontline security controls and what the journey was like in the implementation. The implementation approach started out as a “Big Data for security” program and resulted in six other independent implementations of machine learning driving frontline security controls that have talent implications.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn why model-driven security is here today.
2: See how the implementation approach is not limited to large, sophistcated enterprises.
3: Understand why the growth of unconventional controls using models will continue.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/model-driven-security-its-closer-than-you-think

snippet.title: Confessions of a Cloud Security Convert
snippet.description:
Michael Farnum, Solution Architect Manager, Set Solutions

Michael Farnum had been a network and application security person for many years. He switched roles in the industry right about the same time cloud networking started getting popular, which means he missed the cloud hype train. Now he finds himself in a position where cloud security is a primary concern. Here is what he has learned so far in his journey of converting to the cloud.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn about the conversion process from traditional security to cloud security.
2: Understand the areas where traditional and cloud security differ and are similar.
3: Enjoy a fun talk that shows that the conversion is not terrible.

https://www.rsaconference.com/videos/confessions-of-a-cloud-security-convert

snippet.title: Humans and Data Don’t Mix: Best Practices to Secure Your Cloud
snippet.description:
Stephen Schmidt, Vice President and Chief Information Security Officer, Amazon Web Services

While the causes of outages are varied, human error far outpaces all hardware failures. The risk of humans touching sensitive data is clear, but the tools, techniques and risk-mitigation strategies lag behind current realities. Stephen Schmidt, AWS CISO, will share hard-earned lessons around potential gaps in your security plan, along with steps to lessen potential angles of attack.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn how to put a plan in place that takes advantage of pattern recognition.
2: Discover how to consider your own security blind spots with ways to self-audit.
3: See how to evaluate even well-intentioned security misconfigurations.

snippet.description:
James Wickett, Head of Research, Signal Sciences

All organizations want to go faster and decrease friction in their cloud software delivery pipeline. Infosec has an opportunity to change their classic approach from blocker to enabler. This talk will discuss hallmarks of CI/CD and some practical examples for adding security testing across different organizations. The talk will cover emergent patterns, practices and toolchains that bring security to the table.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn the emerging patterns for security in CI/CD pipelines.
2: Receive a pragmatic security toolchain for CI/CD to use in your organization.
3: Understand the real meaning of DevSecOps is without all the hype.

snippet.description:

What do you do when your CISO asks you for a 10-year cybersecurity strategy? Cybersecurity strategies typically address shorter time frames due to the dynamic technology environment and threat actors' abilities to quickly implement advanced technologies. This session will discuss the development of a 10-year strategy using a combination of bottom-up, top-down and scenario planning approaches.

snippet.description:
Sarah Squire, Senior Technical Architect, Ping Identity

Can you describe the value of identity management using only the thousand most common words in the English language? In the style of Randall Munroe’s “Thing Explainer,” you can learn how to explain important identity concepts using simple words. Identity is incredibly important in today’s market, and the ability to express that importance to nontechnical people is critical.

Learning Objectives:
1: Help your company understand what identity is and why they should invest in it.
2: Explain to your stakeholders that investment in identity provides clear benefits.
3: Gain a common vocabulary to discuss identity with peers and experts in the field.

snippet.description:
Chester Wisniewski, Principal Research Scientist, SOPHOS

We often hear that malware attacks are characteristic of country Y and nation-state X. Some companies even restrict connections to and from certain countries. Does this work? Chester Wisniewski used the data from SophosLabs to look at where the threats are coming from and whether location matters. This talk will present his findings along with advice on how threat location data can aid security policies.

Learning Objectives:
1: Dispel the myth that blocking traffic from country X is an effective strategy.
2: Find things in the data observed that can aid in effective policy creation.
3: Discuss the usefulness of attribution as part of a threat mitigation strategy.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18/agenda/sessions/10296-Does-Malware-Have-Citizenship-Who's-Infecting-Us-and-Does-It-Matter

snippet.description:
Candid Wueest, Threat Researcher, Symantec

Voice activated smart assistants built into dedicated, stationary devices, such as Amazon Echo, Google Home and Apple’s HomePod, are increasingly being found in homes around the globe. This talk will analyze the risks associated with using such smart devices. Learn how they can be tricked into revealing data, setting alarms at 2 AM, or being deactivated remotely.

Learning Objectives:
1: Understand the risks associated with smart voice assistant devices.
2: Learn the most likely attack vectors and the corresponding severity.
3: Learn how to secure voice assistant devices through configuration.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18/agenda/sessions/9191-My-Voice-Is-Your-Command-The-Perils-of-Smart-Voice-Assistants

We all know that illicit activity takes place on the dark web, but very little has been done to help industry leaders understand how illicit marketplaces affect various industries, both from a cybersecurity and an economic perspective. This session will delve into how key US industries are affected by illicit marketplaces and what leaders should be considering in light of this growing phenomena.

1: Educate the audience on how the dark web affects different industries.

snippet.description:
Itsik Mantin, Lead Scientist, Imperva

Dolphin attack and kangaroos that confuse self-driving cars present cyberthreats on AI systems. Like other notable technologies, AI systems are getting security traction and are found to leave undefined edge cases—the material from which cyberattacks are made. Based on experience, this session will provide effective tips for secure incorporation of learning technology in adversarial environments.

Learning Objectives:
1: Learn the cyber-lifecycle and use wider perspective on security and technology.
2: Assessment and mitigation of the risk that comes with AI technology.
3: Better understanding of secure incorporation of AI technology.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us18/agenda/sessions/9498-AI-Deception-Fooling-Artificial-Intelligence-Is-Easier-than-You-Think

snippet.description:
Christopher D. Young, Chief Executive Officer, McAfee

The literal hijacking of air travel changed the ways in which the world connects. What can we learn from the Underwear Bomber and the rule of 3-1-1? Cybersecurity’s equivalent of the federal air marshal is the CISO and SecOps manager, but cybercriminals increasingly corrupt or control our flight manifest. It’s time to we learn from the past in order to go farther, faster in protecting the digital world. It’s an idea whose time has come, because what matters now, is that now matters more than ever.

snippet.description:

snippet.title: Australian Cyber-Engagement: Global in Perspective, Regional in Focus
snippet.description:
Dr Tobias Feakin, Australian Ambassador for Cyber Affairs

We live in the most excitingly interconnected era in human history. Instantaneous communications, transactions and access to information keep our economies growing, infrastructure working, governments enabled and social capital flourishing. There is scarcely a foreign policy issue without a cyber-component, from influence campaigns during elections, cyber-enabled IP theft, transnational cybercrime, online censoring freedom of expression to digital trade, e-commerce and social enablement. As a result, cyber-affairs have shifted from being technical, niche issues to a key strategic foreign policy issue, which demands increasing government attention. However, governments cannot address the opportunities and challenges of cyberspace alone. The Internet is fundamental to the private sector, civil society and consumers, all of whom must coordinate closely to reap the benefits offered by emerging digital technologies. Led by the ambassador for Cyber Affairs, Australia’s international cyber-engagement is global in perspective and regional in focus. It centres around six themes: digital trade, cybercrime, cybersecurity, international security, Internet governance, human rights and technology for development. The ambassador is responsible for coordinating Australia’s capacity building activities across government, private sector and civil society to ensure we all benefit from a free, open and secure cyberspace in the Indo-Pacific region and beyond.

https://www.rsaconference.com/events/ap17/agenda/sessions/5543-australian-cyber-engagement-global-in-perspective

snippet.title: Ransomware Spotlight | RSAC 2017
snippet.description:
As one of the favorite campaigns of cybercriminals this year, ransomware has blown up. Crypto-ransomware in particular has been a major concern of top organizations attempting to safeguard sensitive and vital customer data. Particularly, the internet of things is especially vulnerable to crypto ransomware attacks. For instance, the difference between losing data on a hard drive is devastating — but loosing a life to a data breach or hack of a pacemaker takes ransomware concerns to a new level. Presenters at RSAC 2017 delve into these topics and discuss the ins and outs of cybersecurity in the age of ransomware.

snippet.title: Securing Internet of Things | IoT Security Compilation | RSAC 2017
snippet.description:

When everything starts becoming a computer, and we begin connecting more and more devices, large vulnerabilities become more difficult to ignore. Connected devices can be programmed to do anything -- including receiving malware and infecting nearby connected devices. One way to solve this problem: start securing Internet of Things devices now -- before they become ubiquitous in our daily lives and critical infrastructure.

https://www.rsaconference.com/

snippet.title: Privacy Spotlight | RSAC 2017
snippet.description:

Protecting our privacy remains a pressing, global concern: especially where democracy intersects with privacy. Violations of privacy come with hefty penalties, but are we prepared for the larger discussions of what privacy means with so many organizations using our data? Talks at RSAC 2017 provided a number of perspectives on what privacy means, what people are willing to give up, and just how complex the conversation of security and privacy has become.

snippet.description:

Understanding privacy and data protection in the region can be dizzying. However, the APEC Privacy Framework is beginning to bring some uniformity to the region and has made great strides in recent years. snippet.title: Five Truisms of Internet Security That Apply to the Broader World
snippet.description:
Bruce Schneier, CTO IBM Resilient & Special Advisor to IBM Security, presents a compelling argument about the regulations needed for IoT in his talk at RSAC 2017. He argues that when software permeates every aspect of our lives, everything becomes a computer. This leads to computer security becoming ""everything security."" Our immediate security threats are greater as a result -- cyber threats are now real-world threats. We're creating an internet that senses, thinks and acts. In essence, together we are creating a world-size robot without even realizing it. We have largely left computer security to the market. This is changing as the effects of the failures are now too great. 

Five truisms of Internet security that we need to take to the broader world:
1 - Most software is poorly written and insecure.
2 - The extensibility of computerized systems means that everything can be used against us.
3 - The complexity of computerized systems result in new insecurities.
4 - There are new vulnerabilities in the inter-connections.
5 - Computers and networks are vulnerable in different ways.

snippet.description:

Algorithms need to be adaptable as security professionals constantly deploy changes and patches and usage behavior changes daily. With that, it's well known that attackers evolve their tactics just as quickly as patches and updates occur. Russinovich goes through several case studies that explain and explore the components of a Machine Learning system, and how multiple iterations can classify subsets of data to produce successful Machine Learning algorithms.

The second case study explores how to detect malware for today, not yesterday. He closes with his "Attack Disruption Checklist" and he encourages the industry to share best practices broadly.

snippet.title: Captain Unhook: How to Bypass Everything… Literally
snippet.description:

1) Unhooking "Captain Unhook"
2) Boyson: Network Device Ransomware 
3) BIOS Ransomware

McClure dives into the anatomy of a hack—from the modules being loaded into the process all the way down to comparing the clean and current versions. In user-land, malicious processes have the same access to hooks as the security products installed to protect the system.

McClure also goes through a PoisonTap: where eventhough the box is locked, a hacker can plug in and exploit the system. Using the refresh feature powered by Java Script, a Raspberry Pi Zero can be hacked where the Raspberry Pi becomes a network gateway and ransomware can be deployed.

McClure also touches on why BIOS hacks are a common go-to for hackers: updates are so infrequent that systems can be infected for years with little reprieve.

snippet.description:

Sam Pfeifle Publications Director, International Association of Privacy Professionals
Gregory Reid CEO, InFuture LLC

For decades, information security functions have fought for the responsibility to monitor the flow of information through the organization, in paper and digital formats, throughout its entire life cycle, and to determine the existence and accuracy of data classification. This effort has largely been successful. However, if all data flows through security’s filters, it is incumbent upon security professionals to implement the proper controls to ensure personal data is properly collected for its intended use, either to own that responsibility or, at a minimum, to flag potential issues for compliance, marketing and privacy functions. These types of considerations are new to many in the security profession, and this situation is creating an environment rife with blind spots. In this session, we’ll explore the top blind spots and how to mitigate them.

snippet.title: Webcast: Data Protection and Breach Readiness - How to Stay Secure
snippet.description:
http://www.rsaconference.com/videos/webcast-data-protection-and-breach-readiness-how-to-stay-secure

The threat level has never been higher. As recent headlines attest, no company, organization or government agency is immune to targeted attacks by persistent, skilled adversaries. Their unprecedented success has led many to question the efficacy of solely prevention-focused countermeasures. Rather, a more modern approach includes a multi-layer strategy in which early detection, attack containment and recovery measures are considered together. Having processes in place to detect, mitigate, respond to and remediate the impact of such attacks is imperative for all organizations from startups to global enterprises.  For the past eight years the Online Trust Alliance has published guidance on data protection and breach readiness including a broad set of operational and technical best practices to help protect company’s and customers’ personal data. A key to success is moving from a compliance perspective to one of stewardship. This perspective recognizes the long term impact to a brand, the importance of consumer trust and implications and considerations with vendors and business partners.  In this session you will hear highlights from OTA’s 2016 Data Protection and Breach Readiness Guide with specific advice on actions all organizations should take.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/videos/webcast-data-protection-and-breach-readiness-how-to-stay-secure#sthash.UEG1z53V.dpuf

Co-Founders Gloria Moskowitz-Sweet & Erica Pelavin of My Digital TAT2 discuss the conversations parents can have with their children to help them be ethical, safe and responsible consumers and producers of digital media. 

As part of RSA Conference’s goal to expand its CyberSafety: Kids philanthropic outreach program, RSAC hosted a one-day event, The CyberSmart: Parents Education Workshop, prior to the kick-off of Conference week.  The event provided an overview to parents and caregivers on how to best support and secure their child’s online activities. This CyberSafety video is a recording of one of the workshop presentations.

Website: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/rsac-cyber-safety/cybersmart-parents

• Themselves (sexting, social media, sharing personal information)

snippet.description:

snippet.title: Securing Large-Scale Socio-Technical Systems
snippet.description:
Bruce Schneier, Chief Technology Officer, Resilient Systems
We're creating a world where technology permeates our economies, social interactions, and intimate selves. It's a symbiotic relationship. Facebook, fitness trackers, Uber, smart homes, electronic voting, Internet advertising, and credit card payments: we would have trouble living without these large-scale socio-technical systems, and they couldn't exist without our information. However, they bring a variety of new security threats from users, from outsiders, and from the corporations and governments that control them. This talk looks back at what we've learned from past attempts to secure these systems, and forward at what technologies, laws, regulations, economic incentives, and social norms we need to secure them in the future.
http://www.rsaconference.com/events/us16

snippet.title: Data Center Network Security - How to Navigate Upheaval
snippet.description:
Today’s data center looks and acts much differently than before, especially as cloud technology evolves and more enterprises leverage big data. RSA Conference has teamed up with analyst firm Dell’Oro Group for a webcast discussion to walk through some of the biggest changes to the data center and how they are affecting network security, including:

Network migration to higher speeds
Outsourcing applications to the cloud
Shifting network architecture from static pathways to automated flows that can be dynamically monitored and updated
Listen as Casey Quillin from Dell’Oro Group, Jennifer Lawinski from RSA Conference and Tom McMahon, security engineering manager at Weill Cornell Medical College, discuss these questions and more. What are end users doing now and how will that evolve? We explore the data center in 2016, exploring these questions:

What are the big changes in data center architecture and what security challenges are emerging?
How is network security affected when you move applications to an outsourced data center?

snippet.title: Michael Osborn – “It's Everybody’s Kids”
snippet.description:
As Chief of the Violent Crimes Against Children Unit at the FBI, Michael observes first hand the dangers of the internet our children face. The danger impacts everybody’s children regardless of who you are and and where you live. Internet predators can target your child in your own house.

Michael explains what the very real and dangerous threat of Sextortion is. It is very important that you understand the threats and the vulnerabilities of your children. Only then you can start to protect them by understanding their devices, demonstrating safe behavior and by providing the right tools. You can best protect your child by becoming engaged in their cyber life.

snippet.title: Lance Spitzner — "Show Me How You Use It”
snippet.description:
Lance works to create secure cyber environments. When his four year old registered for a social media site with the help of his grandma and grandpa, they didn’t balk at giving out all their personal info. Children can be very challenging, as are their gaming devices and phones. This raises the question “how can I monitor my kids?” Education and tracking are key. Start when they are very young. Play the clueless parent—they will teach you what to do. Once they are older they are less inclined to listen, and more inclined to deliberately engage in risky behavior. “Ultimately securing your kids is all about education. The more you talk to them the more you’re going to learn.”

See more at: www.rsaconference.com/safe

snippet.title: Detection of Advanced Attacks with a CPU Level Sandbox Technology
snippet.description: First generation OS level Sandbox technology has been around for some time now, allowing organizations to automatically inspect every file passing through their perimeter. Since the introduction of the sandbox concept, the attackers have developed a wide array of evasion techniques, designed to allow their attack to bypass the sandbox inspection and reach the target systems. However, there is another point in time during the infection process that can always be detected if you know what to look for, and is virtually impossible to evade: the Exploit phase. In this session, we will elaborate on a new approach – a CPU level sandbox that can better detect the most advanced attacks, even when they deploy evasion techniques - by monitoring the CPU activity while the exploit occurs.

snippet.title: Securing the Next-Generation Data Center
snippet.description: Enterprise data centers are seeing change like never before. As reliance on public clouds and IaaS are becoming more common, buyers need to re-architect their data centers and deploy a security strategy that not only adapts to new network architectures and tremendous performance increases, but one that can also stand up to increasingly powerful and deceptive attacks. This session will address how security can be applied to different workloads within and beyond the Data Center into the public cloud.

snippet.title: Targeted Attacks, APT’s & Cyberwar - A MKT Buzz or a Real Business Threat?
snippet.description: Seems like we hear every day about the latest cyber threats and that the world is falling apart. But is it true? Will these doomsday scenarios ever affect your business or is it just a concern for governments and big organizations? This session will dig into some attacks and what we can learn from them, providing some provocative thoughts for better risk management.

snippet.title: Cloud Without Borders: Paving the Way for Global Security and Privacy
snippet.description: Technology innovation is changing the way we conduct business and our lives in ways that are hard to predict. Cloud technologies are changing our networks and how we communicate in this hyper connected world, bringing security and privacy to the forefront. Philippe discusses how we can leverage the cloud as a new foundation for cyber security to ensure data security and sovereignty across borders.

snippet.title: Getting Ahead of Cybercrime
snippet.description: In most organizations, cyber threats are increasing faster than the ability to implement security improvements. Even organizations employing good cyber practices are being penetrated — advanced organizations plan for it. So in an environment where you can be under cyber attack and not even know, what can you do? EY believes that to get ahead of cybercrime you need to focus on a three-stage strategy: Activate, Adapt, Anticipate.

snippet.title: The Game Has Changed
snippet.description: Based on the breaches of the past couple of years, it’s obvious that the way our industry has been doing security isn’t working. The adversary continues to get through even “next generation" defenses and what’s worse, too often they do so undetected for months or even years. As the perimeter continues to dissolve under the onslaught of mobile and cloud technologies, enterprises need to realize that the game has changed and that the only way to escape today’s vicious cycle of prevention and remediation is to change our mindset toward security operations.

snippet.title: Quick Look: Security Risks in SDN and Other New Software Apps
snippet.description: More software - web 2.0, HTML5, Cloud, Mobile, and now IOT and SDN ... Today's number one cyber-risk is the least understood and least prevented; yet as more software is deployed, hackers continue to find new ways to attack via our software apps, to steal our data and money, to disrupt or hijack our systems. We look at some new advanced cyber risks regarding SDN and ICS-IOT in particular.

snippet.title: 2013: Security in Knowledge
snippet.description:
This is the opening video from RSA Conference 2013.

Theme:
The Gutenberg Printing Press. Data by itself is nothing but a collection of facts and figures, letters and numbers. However, when ignited by understanding and context, data can become so much more. In 1440, Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith by profession, completed his invention of the printing press, which sparked a revolution in the way people see and describe the world they live in. This collection of wooden and metal letters, regarded as one of the most influential inventions of the second millennium, led to the mass distribution of information and a wave of enlightenment that modernized and transformed culture. Today, we live in a digital age where the printed page is becoming obsolete. But we find ourselves amidst our own information revolution. Data has grown big and gets bigger with every digital transaction we make. It also is more accessible than ever, which leads to the questions, “how do we use, secure and share the information that surrounds us?” As we stand in the midst of the change we look back to the time of Gutenberg to find inspiration for the future of security. Knowledge has always been power. Knowledge has always kept us one step ahead of security threats. We’ve found security in knowledge. And just as Gutenberg’s wooden and metal letters sparked the evolution of culture, at RSA Conference 2013, we bring our security insights and perspectives together to ignite the mass of information that surrounds us. 

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.title: 2012: The Great Cipher Mightier Than The Sword
snippet.description:
This is the opening video for RSA Conference 2012.

Theme:
In 17th century France, a religious war raged between the ruling Roman Catholic French and the French Protestants, known as the Huguenots. After intercepting an encrypted letter from the Huguenots to their allies, the Catholics turned to mathematician Antoine Rossignol for help deciphering the message. The information in that letter led to the Catholics’ defeat of the Huguenots and earned Rossignol, along with his son, Bonaventure, the positions of chief cryptographers for the French Court. Under Louis XIV, the Rossignols developed the Great Cipher and ran the Cabinet noir (Black Chamber). Upon their deaths the Great Cipher’s key was lost and it remained indecipherable for two centuries.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.title: 2011: The Adventures of Alice & Bob
snippet.description:
This is the opening video from RSA Conference 2011.

Theme:
Ron Rivest used fictitious placeholder names to explain the RSA encryption method and the many steps involved in the complex system. Alice & Bob were born to make the subject matter easier to grasp – replacing Person A and Person B. Bruce Schneier, author of Applied Cryptography and another forefather of information security, introduced a host of other characters to make technical topics more understandable. This cast of friends and enemies – including Eve the Eavesdropper, Mallory the Malicious Attacker and Walter the Warden, among others – populate Alice & Bob's universe and evolved into common parlance in cryptography and computer security.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.title: 2010: The Rosetta Stone
snippet.description:
This is the opening video from RSA Conference 2010.

Theme:
Mysterious hieroglyphs line ancient Egyptian tomb walls, leading the Pharaohs to the afterlife. For thousands of years, their meaning remained shrouded in secrecy, the ability to decode the complex writing lost to time. In 1799, the chance discovery of a large, badly damaged stele – known as the Rosetta Stone – along the Nile delta changed everything. For more than two decades, the greatest minds in the scientific and intellectual communities compared the 14 lines Hieroglyphic, 32 lines Demotic, and 54 lines ancient Greek on the stone, sharing insights and building on each other’s work. The big breakthrough came in 1822 with the realization that each hieroglyph could represent a sound or concept, depending on context. The Rosetta Stone’s message was no longer veiled by obscurity–the ancients’ marks could be deciphered and the doors opened to modern Egyptology.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.title: 2009: Edgar Allen Poe
snippet.description:
This is the opening video from RSA Conference 2009.

Theme:
Poe was fascinated by cryptography, which he often treated in his journalism and fiction. He concealed anagrams and hidden messages in his own poems. His famous story - The Gold Bug - centers on the solution of a cipher, which turns out to be a map to hidden private treasure. In 1839 Poe conducted his own cryptographic challenge. Writing in Alexander's Weekly Messenger, Poe challenged his readers to submit their cryptographs to him, asserting that he would solve them all. A year later Poe wrote an article for Graham's Magazine titled "A Few Words on Secret Writing". In it, he offered to give a free subscription to the magazine to anyone who would send him a cipher he could not crack. Poe ended the contest six months later, claiming to have solved all of the 100 ciphers sent to him. He concluded by publishing two ciphers ostensibly sent in by Mr. W. B. Tyler, praising their author as a "gentleman whose abilities we highly respect" and challenging readers to solve them. There the ciphers remained until 1985 when Professor Louis Renza of Dartmouth College suggested that Tyler was actually a double for Poe himself. Renza's theory was later elaborated by Shawn Rosenheim in his book The Cryptographic Imagination: Secret Writing from Edgar Allan Poe to the Internet. In it, Rosenheim points to the likelihood that the ciphers were placed in the magazine by Poe himself as a final challenge to his readers.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.title: 2008: Alan Mathison Turing
snippet.description:
This is the opening video from RSA Conference 2008.

Theme:
Alan Mathison Turing (1912-1954) was a British cryptographer, mathematician, logician, philosopher and biologist. Experts and historians agree that Alan Turing had a deeper understanding of the vast potential of computer science than anyone in his era, and is often considered the father of modern computer science. During World War II, Turing was part of the team of scientists working at Britain's Bletchley Park Government and Cipher School and responsible for building the Bombe, a complex electromechanical machine designed to decipher secret codes and transmissions. The Bombewas the starting point for Turing to develop more advanced computer prototypes throughout his career. His most recognized invention, the Universal Machine(or Turing Machine), was a flashpoint in the evolution of computers because it read a series of "ones and zeroes" from a paper tape, then triggered the steps required to perform automated tasks. His work inspired the ACM A.M. Turing Award, which is widely considered to be the computing world's equivalent to the Nobel Prize. Turing also explored the relationship between machines and living organisms, opening the door to Artificial Intelligence.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.title: 2007: Leon Batista Alberti
snippet.description:
This is the opening video from RSA Conference.

Theme:
Leon Battista Alberti was an illustrious mind of the Renaissance period whose scientific and cultural influence surpassed his brief life span. A painter, poet, philosopher, musician, architect and "Father of Western Cryptology", Alberti invented the first published polyalphabetic cipher in 1466. His cipher disk contained two alphabets, one on a fixed outer ring, and the other on a rotating disk, and is the cipher design to which most of today's systems of cryptography belong: polyalphabetic substitution. Alberti's polyalphabetic cipher was, at least in principle, the most significant advance in cryptography since Julius Caesar's time and marked a great stride forward in cryptology.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/about/themes#sthash.qY7dOLI8.dpuf

snippet.description:
Effective cyber security requires that governments, private companies, and NGOs work together to understand threats in cyberspace, and to share information and capabilities for mitigating them. With the burgeoning ‘Smart City’ development in Asia, this becomes even more pertinent. Without this collaboration, national and economic security would be in jeopardy.

snippet.title: Quick Look: The Enemy You Know
snippet.description: Most organizations consider the insider threat a single type of actor, when it is a grouping of several distinct adversary types. A variety of defenses must be deployed in order to be effective against the different types. This session will articulate the different types of adversaries through case study analysis and provide attendees with actionable tactics to effectively defend against each type.

snippet.title: Quick Look: You’ve Done Everything Right, and Still There’s a Breach. Now What?
snippet.description:
The drumbeat of newspaper headlines trumpeting the next big data breach shows how precarious even the best of cyber defenses are. The companies did everything they were supposed to do, and still lost their data. It’s clear that the cybersecurity playbook needs to be rewritten. Leveraging insights from a wide swath of IT professionals, this presentation will cover some of the key elements that need to be in our new playbook.

snippet.description: This session is the result of a yearlong study of the most recent ICS/SCADA vulnerabilities that affected industrial control systems and critical infrastructure. snippet.description: Asian organizations are more frequently targeted by advanced threat actors than their western counterparts. Why? This session will share our latest detailed findings--including previously unreleased research--about types of companies targeted, techniques being used by nation state and hacktivist actors, among others, and how your organization can avoid becoming a victim.

Jim discusses the challenges, opportunities and solutions to provide assurance in the cloud, how enterprises are managing risks in the cloud today, the problems that remain for industry to solve and highlights the efforts undertaken by CSA to build the trust in the cloud.

snippet.title: Quick Look: ShadowOS - Modifying the Android OS for Mobile Application Testing
snippet.description:
Most penetration testers know the headaches of testing mobile applications. Challenges like certificate pinning and wondering what files are being written to the device while the app is in use. Since Android is open source, you create your own custom OS that takes the guess work out of your assessment. By doing this, you can monitor HTTP/HTTPS traffic, SQL Lite queries, file access and more.

See more at: http://www.rsaconference.com/events/ap15/agenda/sessions/2046/shadowos-modifying-the-android-os-for-mobile#sthash.VXBFKZu6.dpuf

snippet.title: Leadership Lessons of History: American Presidents
snippet.description: Doris Kearns Goodwin shares in-depth analysis of the U.S. presidency, which she has studied for more than four decades. Drawing from her bestselling biographies of Lyndon Johnson, Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, Franklin Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln, Goodwin brings the past alive, delivering an insider’s look at the captivating stories that illuminate the inner complexities of our most fascinating leaders.

snippet.title: The Four Horsemen of Mobile Security
snippet.description:
Hackers today apply covert and persistent techniques to attack mobile devices. While other PC endpoints have ton of security solutions such as IPS, IDS, Firewall, AV installed, mobile devices are comparatively “naked.” Hackers know this and attack mobile devices on several fronts - Physical, Network, Malware and by exploiting known and unknown vulnerabilities.  Attend this presentation with Skycure to learn about the latest threats on mobile devices from the team who uncovered No iOS Zone, Malicious Profiles, and HTTP Request Hijacking. 

In this webcast, security professionals will hear mobile security experts Adi Sharabani and Yair Amit describe the current threat landscape for mobile devices and discuss security strategies. They will:

- Describe and demonstrate emerging mobile security threats: from physical, through network and up to application level
- Share best practices from around the globe on how to secure the mobile fleet
- Help organizations create a step-by-step mobile security plan

The threats against mobile devices are diverse, requiring security professionals to adopt a different mindset and strategy. Our best defense is to be prepared for all eventualities.

Understand current threats and vulnerabilities as well as how enterprises are responding.  Results will include top threats faced,as well as information on controls, skills employers are looking for, security organizational structures and incident plans.

It may look like a solitary sport, but it takes a team.” Her ability to overcome challenges is an inspiration to all.

snippet.description:
Stuart McClure, Brian Wallace

snippet.description:
Amit Chatterjee
Executive Vice President, Enterprise Solutions and Technology Group, CA Technologies

In the application economy, enterprises face huge growth opportunities and expanded business risk. To win, it is imperative to rethink security as both enabling and protecting, and going from NO to KNOW. Learn how this new approach to security allows organizations to thrive by successfully navigating the disruptive trends of the unwired enterprise, ambient data and API-assembled applications.

snippet.title: Security in an Age of Catastrophic Risk
snippet.description:
Bruce Schneier
Chief Technology Officer, Resilient Systems

In cyberspace and out, we're increasingly confronting extremely-low-probability, extremely-high-damage attacks. Protecting against these sorts of risks requires new ways of thinking about security; one that emphasizes agility and resilience, while avoiding worst-case thinking.

snippet.title: The Six Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques and What's Coming Next
snippet.description:
John Pescatore, Ed Skoudkis, Johannes Ullrich, Mike Assante 

What are the most dangerous new attack techniques? How do they work? How can you stop them? What's coming next? In this fast-paced briefing you'll hear answers to those questions from the three people best positioned to know the answers: the Head of the Internet Storm Center, the top hacker expert/teacher in the U.S., and the top expert on cyber attacks on industrial control systems

snippet.title: You Can’t Stop What You Can’t See
snippet.description:
Jared Myers, Grant Geyer
The advanced threats facing organizations today – across all industries and company sizes – are sophisticated and outmatch most organizations’ security capabilities. But it doesn’t have to be that way. We will begin our session by revealing a previously unknown threat actor and its TTPs based on new RSA research. We will use this research to set the stage for a discussion about the world of advanced threats – including individual organizations, their TTPs, and the ecosystems in which they operate – and the daunting realities facing organizations today. From that foundation, we will move into a discussion about why traditional security programs are increasingly failing to detect and prevent these attacks, focusing predominantly on two factors – visibility and understanding. Traditional security tools such as SIEM are not able to provide the fine-grained visibility necessary to monitor for and detect the TTPs of advanced threat actors. The most recent Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report indicates that SIEM, the source of visibility for the vast majority of organizations, was only able to see 1% of advanced threats. We need to evolve our approach to visibility to ensure comprehensive visibility. We need to see everything to make sure nothing is missed. But visibility without understanding what you are seeing is worthless, as many organizations learned over the past year when their advanced security systems were able to see advanced threats but not make sense of them. We must move to a security approach that relies on strong analytics to make sense of and understand the visibility our advanced systems can give us. We will end with an overview of the steps organizations can take to review their own visibility and analytical capabilities and begin closing the gap between their current state and desired end state based on their security maturity level, staffing, and resources.

snippet.title: There Are No Domestic Cyber Issues: US & UK Leaders on Global Partnership
snippet.description:
Michael Daniel, Natalie Black
Cyber is a global team sport. (There’s no such thing as a domestic cyber issue)  That means we need to build effective partnerships to do big things in cyber.   Given the breadth and diversity of stakeholders, building effective partnerships is a challenge.   The good news is, partnerships are maturing and we are seeing results.  Cyber leaders for the US and the UK will discuss recent gains and the outlook for the future.

snippet.title: Dan Geer on the Future of Security
snippet.description:
Dan Geer
CISO, In-Q-Tel
The security landscape is rapidly changing, with many emerging consequences of highly inner-connected devices and changing attitudes toward government, privacy and legislation. All of these will help to shape our industry. Dan Geer weighs in with his thoughts on the current state of information security, where we are headed and some of the stumbling blocks we may find along the way.

snippet.title: Patching Exploits with Duct Tape: Bypassing Mitigations and Backward Steps
snippet.description:
James Lyne, Stephen Sims
The sale of exploits and bug bounty programs are at an all-time high, as is their use by cyber criminals. OS vendors, such as Microsoft have progressively implemented a gigantic number of controls to stem the bleeding. Learn how attackers side step mitigations in accessible live demonstrations. New to exploitation or want to learn about the latest mitigations? Come along and learn more!

snippet.title: The Sophisticated Attack Myth: Hiding Unsophisticated Security Programs
snippet.description:
Ira Winkler, Araceli Treu Gomes
All recent, significant hacking incidents have been attributed to “sophisticated attacks.” The reality is that such attacks are the new normal. Sophisticated attack claims reflect unsophisticated security programs. This presentation will analyze recent attacks and show how they could have been prevented, and recommend methods for strengthening security programs to stop those attacks in the future

snippet.title: Want to be Secure in the Cloud? Build a Casino
snippet.description:
Joan Delilah Pepin,
Vice President of Security/CISO, Sumo Logic 

Cloud security requires a new way of thinking. Companies have to take the same approach as casinos and trade control for scalability. Rather than regulating every single gambler, casinos instead use statistics to ensure proper gaming and that the house always wins. Sumo Logic CISO Joan Pepin will show how moving to the cloud means your house always wins in the end

snippet.title: Phishing for the Phoolish: Why Hackers Love Gilligans and Their Best Lures
snippet.description:
Grant Asplund,
Director of Evangelism, Blue Coat Systems

Hackers just love the foolish. The vast majority of users today are not technically savvy and do not understand the infrastructure that supports and drives the Internet. This session will combine humor and current research from nearly 80M users, to highlight how hackers are taking advantage of the uninformed to successfully expand their reach and ways to limit hacker's success.

snippet.title: General Alexander: Life After the NSA
snippet.description:
General Keith Alexander - Former Director, NSA, Ted Schlein - Partner, Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers

With data breaches now a daily occurrence, cybersecurity experience from the NSA is in higher demand than ever before. The agency has become a breeding ground for security entrepreneurs. In this session, Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein interviews former NSA Director General Keith Alexander on life after the NSA and his transition to the private sector.

snippet.title: Hot Topics in Privacy: A Conversation with Facebook, Google and Microsoft
snippet.description:
Trevor Hughes - President & Chief Executive Officer, IAPP, Brendon Lynch - Chief Privacy Officer, Microsoft, Erin Egan - Chief Privacy Officer, Policy, Facebook, Keith Enright - Director, Privacy Legal Team, Google

The explosion of social media, mobile devices and internet sharing has pushed privacy to the forefront of consumer’s consciousness. With new developments, including the Right to Be Forgotten, big data and the consumer cloud, there is no end to privacy issues facing society. Join privacy leaders from Facebook, Google and Microsoft, as they explore the hot topics faced by leaders in this space

snippet.title: Stop Selling and Start Marketing Your Information Security Program
snippet.description:
Thom Langford,
Chief Security Information Officer, Sapient

How effective is your InfoSec program, really? Learn how a single change in approach and attitude to your Infosec Awareness program can have dramatic effects on your organization's security stance. See how professional marketers focus on lifestyle rather than products, and understand how you can apply that to your own program with dramatic effect, driving high levels of engagement and support

snippet.title: Assume Breach: An Inside Look at Cloud Service Provider Security
snippet.description:
Mark Russinovich
Chief Technology Officer, Azure-Microsoft 

Microsoft uses the three classic pillars in its Azure security strategy: Protect. Defend. Respond. This talk describes them from an insider’s perspective, with first-hand examples of how we use isolation and JiT to protect against compromised users, penetration test live services and leverage analytics to detect malicious activities, and integrate data sharing to rapidly respond to incidents.

snippet.title: The Economics of Online Identity: 6 Buzzwords to Impress your Boss
snippet.description:
Mike Garcia,
Deputy Director, NSTIC

session explores the host of vexing economic phenomena preventing markets from doing what many of us would like them to do in identity. Through demonstrations, a description of how human behavior impacts online choices, and presentation of case studies, attendees will learn about the apparent stubbornness of markets, and will walk away with improved tools to analyze and describe market forces

snippet.title: The Sound of Metrics
snippet.description:
David Scott,
Chief, Software Development,  CSG Invotas

Can Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony predict future cyber events? Does jazz music have anything in common with STIX models? Both sound and security events have timbre, style, structure, volume, rhythm, and history. We explore the ways musical concepts such as motifs, chord structures, and improvisation enhance our understanding of security and help us predict future cyber events.

snippet.title: Hacking Exposed: Beyond the Malware
snippet.description:
George Kurtz, Dmitri Alpervitch, Elia Zaitsev

What do you do when adversaries don't use any malware or exploits? This session will demonstrate cutting edge techniques that we've observed from the most recent intrusions that are super stealthy and don't leave any malware footprint in your environment. In the typical raw Hacking Exposed style, we demonstrate these attacks and provide relevant countermeasures for detection and response.

snippet.title: Security Humanitarianism: Extraordinary Examples of Tech Improving Lives
snippet.description:
Davi Ottenheimer,
Senior Director of Trust, EMC

This presentation runs through some extraordinary examples of information security projects built for organizations to improve global health and welfare. Find out how data security creates trusted foundations for humanitarian projects in dangerous environments around the world. Disasters impact each of us more than ever from more data, with more detail, at a faster pace. Hear how you can help

snippet.title: Closing the Gap: Steps to Satisfy the Demand for Security Talent
snippet.description:
Jacob West
Chief Architect, Security Products, NetSuite

The talent gap in security is huge and growing. Tools compensate in some cases, but skilled people are critical to managing security risk. With nearly half of security roles vacant, organizations must develop talent inside and out. This session offers practical steps you can take today—ranging from adopt-a-professor to highlighting security in every job description—that will help close the gap.

snippet.title: Hack the Planet: Some Men Just Want to Watch the World Burn
snippet.description:
Mark Arena
Chief Executive Officer, Intel 471 Inc

Hack the Planet is a sophisticated group that aren’t hacktivists nor financially motivated cyber criminals. They compromise their targets either directly or through upstream service providers. In one instance, their target was an Internet Relay Chat network and they broke in via their virtual server provider. This is the story of Hack the Planet, their offshoots and intrusion TTPs.

snippet.title: How Much Does Your Ox Weigh?: Crowdsource Your Way to Data Protection
snippet.description:
Maor Goldberg
Chief Executive Officer, Whitebox Security

Mathematician Francis Galton discovered that the mean of 800 participants’ guesses about an ox’s weight was closer than any individual guess or the median. The crowd - 1,197 pounds, actual was 1,198. The concept of crowdsourced data security is based on the same principle: the collective intelligence of the crowd strengthens security by accelerating the elimination of risk at increased accuracy.

snippet.title: When IT Threats Meet OT Innocence
snippet.description:
Udi Solomon
Vice President Product, ThetaRay

Since the inception of the Internet, billions of humans have come online, dragging all manner of crime into cyberspace. But this was only Phase I of an ongoing digital revolution. Phase II:  ‘things’ are coming online, not humans! This fascinating session will give attendees timely insight about a connecting world of OT, and its exposure to IT threats, miles ahead in scale and sophistication

snippet.title: 2014 Hack, Exploit and Malware Retrospective...And the Worry List Ahead
snippet.description:
James Lyne
Global Head of Security Research, Sophos

This fast-paced RSAC Studio session looks at some of the major incidents of the last year—how they worked and what we should have learned from them. See the inner workings of the top nasties of 2014, and hear the worry list for the year ahead. 

See more at: https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us15/agenda/sessions/1966/2014-hack-exploit-and-malware-retrospective-and-the#sthash.0byrw9ml.dpuf

snippet.title: Fail-safe the Human Pysche to Advance Security and Privacy
snippet.description:
Theresa Payton
CEO, Co-Author and Former White House CIO, Fortalice Solutions, LLC

We are in now in an era of the “loss of innocence and privacy.”  Everyone from grandma, to Oscar winners, and major corporations are targets for cyber criminals.  Everyone is a target, because of who they are, whom they know, what they do, or even the fact that they are connected to the Internet. If we want to solve today and tomorrow's problems, we have to rethink how we deliver security

snippet.title: Sun Tzu Meets the Cloud: Everything Is Different, Nothing Has Changed
snippet.description:
Sean Jennings
Co-Founder and SVP of Solutions Architecture, Virtustream
In this session, Sean Jennings, SVP Solutions Architecture at Virtustream, will propose a 21st-century cloud security strategy under the timeless context of Sun Tzu’s Art of War. He will discuss the need for provider transparency, continuous risk monitoring and compliance - including tools/approaches for effective Enterprise Risk Management, Cyber Situational Awareness and Compliance Management.

snippet.title: There’s an App for That: How the Future of Privacy Will Be Consumer-Driven
snippet.description:
David Gorodyansky
Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder, AnchorFree

We have apps for everything, why not privacy? Consumers will demand privacy be automatic rather than an afterthought, especially as more mainstream brands report major hacks. Keeping data private will be the next must-have for companies that want to thrive in an increasingly mobile world. AnchorFree CEO David Gorodyansky discusses how cybercrime will only increase the consumer demand for privacy.

snippet.title: A Short History of Attacks on Finance
snippet.description:
Maurits Lucas
InTELL Business Director, Fox-IT

From ZeuS to Shylock, from kit malware to MAAS, private groups and open groups, from POS malware to espionage, from Gribodemon to organized crime, this talk is a rollercoaster ride through the history of financial cybercrime. In the fashion of Bill Bryson’s “Short history”, this talk fills you in on 9 years of cybercrime, including the soap like events around actors.

snippet.title: Amazing True Crimes and the Lessons They Can Teach Us
snippet.description:
Mark McGovern 
Chief Executive Officer, Mobile System 7

Bank robbers, thieves and spies will do phenomenal things to get what they want. Indeed, they avoid detection and defenses by doing the unexpected. Attendees will be amazed at the resources and skill used in six audacious real world crimes. More importantly, they'll be amused by how clearly the lessons learned from these apply to cyber defenses today.

snippet.title: The Day My Kids Brought Home Malware
snippet.description:
Kellman Meghu
Head of Americas Security Architects, Check Point Software

Kids are always texting, streaming shows and surfing the web simultaneously. With all of that Internet activity, what type of malware activity do you think you’d find on your home network? This talk gives insight from activity on my network, set up with Enterprise products. Imagine utilizing this technology and finding search patterns of data in your home network – what do you think you’ll find?

snippet.title: Stuck in Patterns - How Your Mind Fools You Every Day
snippet.description:
Doug Kevilus
Owner, Mentalist Doug Kevilus

Our minds have developed in such a way that it changes and distorts what we see, experience, and remember every day. Some of those distortions we will never recognize. Other times, those distortions create severe consequences in our work and personal relationships

snippet.title: 10 Tips for Running an Effective SOC - Buzzfeed Style
snippet.description:
Jeff Caplan
VSOC Operations Manager, Foreground Security

There exists a lot of advice for how to build and run a Security Operations Center (SOC); however, the state of the information security industry is such that what was considered a 'successful' SOC 5 or 10 years ago is not the same today. In this discussion, I will distill some of the most practical tips for running an effective SOC in a humorous way, utilizing both memes and real-life examples.

snippet.description: Become part of the action on Friday as Hugh Thompson interviews some very special guests. Internationally celebrated as one of our finest comedic talents, Alec Baldwin is also highly regarded for his keen intellect, insight and wit. His personal passions range across the cultural spectrum, well outside the narrow lanes of the entertainment industry. Alec will engage with Hugh in an extended 1:1 interview.

snippet.description:
Benjamin Jun
RSA Conference Advisory Board
Director, Mad Scientist Academy

snippet.title: I Am RSA Conference: Happiness
snippet.description: Security professionals share what makes them happy. Doing something they are passionate about, spending time with family and friends. What makes you happy?

snippet.title: I Am RSA Conference: Most Dangerous Threats
snippet.description: There isn’t one single answer. There are many threats, dangerous ones, and we need to do something.  Here is a thought: maybe we are our biggest threat.

snippet.title: I Am RSA Conference: What Color is Your Hat?
snippet.description: The real world is not so simple, and we can’t just call it either black or white.  Hats, at least. Instead of worry about black hat or white hat hackers, we need to think in terms of builders, maintainers, and destroyers.

snippet.title: I Am RSA Conference: Our Mount Rushmore
snippet.description: Information security is full of legends. If we were to erect our very own Mount Rushmore, who should we include? Should it be all cryptographers? Make room for the security geeks and hackers.

snippet.title: Into the Woods: Protecting Our Youth from the Wolves of Cyberspace
snippet.description:
Sandra Toms - VP and Curator, RSA Conference
Lance Spitzner - Research & Community Director, SANS
Michael Osborn - Chief of the Violent Crimes Against Children Unit, FBI
Sharon W. Cooper - MD, FAAP
Alicia Kozakiewicz - President, The Alicia Project

Today's headlines are crowded with stories of kids who fall victim to cybercrimes, including online bullying and predatory behavior. We can't supervise every dark corner of the Internet, so what is the answer? Stricter laws? Aggressive pursuit of offenders? Education of our kids? This keynote panel will discuss challenges and offer solutions designed to ensure the safety of our children.

snippet.title: Advanced Strategies for Defending Against a New Breed of Attacks
snippet.description:
Martin Roesch - Vice President and Chief Architect, Cisco Security Business Group

Business leaders are now tasked with protecting their organizations from the effects of catastrophic attacks that cause significant losses in minutes and take months to discover, contain and remediate. Roesch will outline strategies to evolve security to include new approaches that address incidents efficiently, enable visibility, facilitate appropriate actions and support business growth.

snippet.description: Presented by James Andrew Lewis, Winner: Richard A. Clarke

snippet.title: 2015 Excellence in the Field of Mathematics Award
snippet.description:

The RSA Conference Award for Mathematics recognizes innovation and ongoing contribution to the field of cryptography. The judging committee seeks to acknowledge those nominees who are pioneers in their field, and whose work has applied lasting value. Nominees are affiliated with universities or research labs.

snippet.title: 2015 Excellence in the Field of Public Policy Award
snippet.description:
Presented by James Andrew Lewis, Winner: J. Michael Daniel

The RSA Conference Award for Public Policy is designed to recognize significant contribution and leadership in the field of cyber security public policy. The judging committee seeks to reward nominees who hold elected or appointed office, are associated with public interest organizations or are associated with an organization that has significantly contributed to the development or application of current information security and/or privacy policy.

snippet.title: 2015 Excellence in Information Security Award
snippet.description:
Presented by Dave Martin, Winner: John N. Stewart

The RSA Conference Award for Excellence in Information Security recognizes outstanding achievement in the industry. The judging committee seeks to recognize a security practitioner for their outstanding security program or initiative.

snippet.title: Talking ’bout My Next Generation
snippet.description:
Chris Hoff - Juniper Networks

Who would’ve thought a 50-year-old song would’ve been the perfect descriptor for how cyber security practitioners sometimes feel viewed by the rest of the world? In the immortal words of The Who, “People try to put us down.” Come hear about what’s next for cyber security. The answer might surprise you and “cause a big sensation.” - See more at: https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us15/agenda/sessions/1858/talking-bout-my-next-generation#sthash.HCIZpqDH.dpuf

snippet.title: Quantitative Security: Using Moneyball Techniques to Defend Corporate Networks
snippet.description:
Amit Mital, Symantec

In “Moneyball,” Michael Lewis describes how a sports team used data analytics to field the best possible players. Can this quantitative approach help a company achieve the highest possible level of security? Amit Mital will discuss how advanced data mining on massive amounts of security intelligence will help organizations thwart even the most complex attacks on their systems and information.

snippet.title: Welcome to the New School of Cyber Defense
snippet.description:
Art Gilliland, HP

The old school of cyber defense emphasized securing infrastructure and restricting data flows. But data needs to run freely to power our organizations. The new school of cyber defense calls for security that is agile and intelligent. It emphasizes protecting the interactions between our users, our applications and our data. The world has changed, and we must change the way we secure it.

snippet.description:

Experts share the challenges of and opportunities for receiving funding from venture capitalists, government agencies or Kickstarter campaigns.

snippet.description: Oliver Tavakoli, CTO, Vectra

snippet.title: Enhancing Cloud Trust
snippet.description:
Scott Charney, Microsoft

As pressures to accelerate cloud computing climb higher than ever, relationships between vendors, enterprises and governments have evolved to ones comprised of trust and concern in equal measure. How should companies shape their plans? Join Scott Charney for a review of Microsoft’s cyber security strategy to help leaders innovate aggressively while managing business risk. 

See more at: https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us15/agenda/sessions/1947/enhancing-cloud-trust#sthash.bPJF7ZTe.dpuf

snippet.title: Secretary Jeh Johnson, Department of Homeland Security
snippet.description:
Secretary Jeh C. Johnson, U.S. Department of Homeland Security

The growing number of serious attacks on essential cyber networks is one of the most serious economic and national security threats our nation faces. DHS Secretary Jeh Johnson will discuss the evolving cybersecurity threat and Homeland Security's comprehensive strategy to address it.

snippet.title: Escaping Security's Dark Ages
snippet.description:
Amit Yoran, RSA

We are living in the Dark Ages of security.  We cling to outmoded world views and rely on tools and tactics from the past, and yet we are surprised to find ourselves living in an era of chaos and violence.  We must cast off the past and enter an Age of Enlightenment by pursuing greater visibility into and understanding of our digital world.

See more at: https://www.rsaconference.com/events/us15/agenda/sessions/1946/escaping-securitys-dark-ages#sthash.Cks5zuFA.dpuf

snippet.description:
RSA Conference 2015 is just around the corner and we couldn’t be more excited. This year is shaping up to be the best—and biggest!—RSA Conference yet.

Veterans of the show will be the first to say RSA Conference is more than just keynotes and sessions. Count on having thought-provoking conversations with your peers on the P2P track. The show may feel a little overwhelming, but never fear, we are here to help. Listen to RSA Conference’s general manager Linda Gray for help developing a plan of attack for RSA Conference week. What should you do before you even leave home? What will make the show easier to manage?
